claim_verdicts.evidence: refs/kubernetes-website/.../style/page-content-types.md:9-17: "The Kubernetes documentation follows several types of page content: - Concept - Task - Tutorial - Reference" and "You may also find the Diátaxis documentation framework helpful as a reference for how to write each of these page content types." One official doc set splits its pages four ways and labels them Concept/Task where the framework it cites uses explanation/how-to — the label difference the claim states. The hedges "commonly" and "roughly" stay inside this evidence.

Same page, "Content types": "A tutorial page shows how to accomplish a goal that is larger than a single task. Typically a tutorial page has several sections, each of which has a sequence of steps." and "A task page shows how to do a single thing, typically by giving a short sequence of steps. Task pages have minimal explanation, but often provide links to conceptual topics." "goal larger than a single task", "one named thing", "minimal explanation" are the documented words.

Concept half, same page: "A concept page explains some aspect of Kubernetes ... Typically, concept pages don't include sequences of steps, but instead provide links to tasks or tutorials." Options and defaults: refs/kubernetes-website/.../reference/kubectl/kubectl.md:62,118 "--cache-dir string Default: \"$HOME/.kube/cache\"", "--default-not-ready-toleration-seconds int Default: 300". Errors: refs/dotnet-docs/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-messages/ is a reference set of error pages ("Compiler Error CS0101"). Only "reasons behind the design" reads stronger than "explains some aspect".

No docs root in content/versions.yaml prescribes a reading method or reading speed. I read refs/kubernetes-website/content/en/docs/contribute/style/page-content-types.md and style-guide.md: they say what each page type is for and how to write it, never how fast a reader reaches an entry. Nothing in refs/ measures it. The lesson's wording is hedged ("you will usually get there faster"), so the text does not outrun the absent evidence; kind=opinion, so this verdict does not block approval.

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/index.html carries a bar at the top of the page: "Supported Versions: Current (18) / 17 / 16 / 15 / 14", then "Development Versions: 19 / devel". Each entry links to the same page under /docs/<n>/, i.e. one complete page set per release, switched by a control near the top. That is exactly what the hedged claim says.

On that same bar "Current" resolves to /docs/current/ and is labelled 18, while content/versions.yaml pins data.postgresql version "17" with docs root https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/. A reader who lands on the site's default entry reads release 18, not the release pinned for this course, unless they move the selector.

No docs root in versions.yaml prescribes a triage order for a page that disagrees with a machine. I searched refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt (section 2.2 Conformance and around) and refs/kubernetes-website/content/en/docs/contribute/style/ and found nothing of the kind. The same three candidates do appear in examples/don-hang at stage-0, docs/craft/doc-reading-checklist.md line 23-24 ("sai ở phiên bản của tài liệu, phiên bản của tôi, hay giả định của tôi? Xác định cái nào."), but that file is this lesson's own material, not independent evidence. kind=opinion, non-blocking.

Tag object refs/tags/stage-0 = 664d38a0…, inflated: "tag 291 object ff911b0bc73af1529865b3752ea2ac59942eaaf0 / type commit / tag stage-0", and refs/heads/auto/stage-0 = ff911b0b = the checked-out submodule HEAD, so working-tree reads are tag reads. outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cache-headers.txt first block: "1. the response says how long a cache may reuse it: / HTTP/1.1 200 OK / Cache-Control: max-age=60 / Etag: ...". The header line is printed under the first response, as the lesson says.

docs/craft/doc-reading-checklist.md at stage-0: heading "## Trước khi đọc" is followed by exactly four checkboxes — which kind of information is wanted; which kind this page is ("Trang tra cứu thì tìm, đừng đọc từ đầu"); which version the page is written for and whether a selector exists; which version the reader runs. The lesson's first code block (lines 5-10) is byte-identical to the source after whitespace normalisation.

Same file, lines 29-35: "Tài liệu kỹ thuật dùng một vốn từ hẹp và dùng rất chính xác. Vài chục từ lặp đi lặp lại: *deprecated*, *default*, *required*, *optional*, *idempotent*, *throws*, *unless*, *at least once*, *must*, *should*, *may*." Eleven words, same order as the lesson's second code block; the block is byte-identical to the source after whitespace normalisation.

refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:549-553, section 2.2 Requirements Notation: "The key words \"MUST\", \"MUST NOT\", \"REQUIRED\", \"SHALL\", \"SHALL NOT\", \"SHOULD\", \"SHOULD NOT\", \"RECOMMENDED\", \"NOT RECOMMENDED\", \"MAY\", and \"OPTIONAL\" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here." "when, and only when" is precisely the capitals condition the claim and section 5 assert.

RFC 9110 section 2.2 imports BCP 14; I fetched the imported document https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119: MUST "mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification"; SHOULD "mean that there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course"; MAY "mean that an item is truly optional". Section 5 repeats all three in the same terms. Caveat: RFC 2119 is not itself a docs root in versions.yaml and is not mirrored in refs/rfc.
claim_verdicts.source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119 sections 1, 3, 5, imported by refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt section 2.2

claim_verdicts.evidence: Recurrence across unrelated products is measurable in the mirrors: a case-insensitive search for \bidempotent\b over refs/ returns 70 files spanning refs/rfc (rfc9110, rfc9112), refs/kubernetes-website (generated API reference v1.23-v1.37, concepts, tasks), refs/dotnet-docs, refs/aspnetcore-docs, refs/docker-docs and refs/flutter-website. Fixed meaning is prescribed too: refs/kubernetes-website/.../style/style-guide.md:341-343 "## Kubernetes.io word list — A list of Kubernetes-specific terms and words to be used consistently across the site."

Still working: refs/kubernetes-website/content/en/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy.md:372 "Rule #7: Deprecated behaviors must function for no less than 1 year after their announced deprecation." On its way out, but not always: :19 "a deprecation policy for aspects of the system that are slated to be removed" against :244 "v1 is deprecated in favor of v2, but will not be removed" — which is what the lesson's hedge "often" carries. No longer recommended: :363 "Rule #6: Deprecated CLI elements must emit warnings (optionally disable) when used."

The official half is partly supported: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/index.html heads the page "PostgreSQL 17.11 Documentation" above the version bar. But versions.yaml gives redis as https://redis.io/docs/latest/ and docker as https://docs.docker.com/, neither naming a release, and http as a fixed RFC — so "usually states its version at the top" is a generalisation past the evidence. The blog half is a generalisation about blogs that no docs root and nothing in refs/ measures. kind=opinion; the lesson hedges with "often"/"usually"; non-blocking.

No docs root in versions.yaml documents machine-translation behaviour and nothing in refs/ measures it. The mechanism is checkable — refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt section 2.2 ties the requirement levels to the words "when, and only when, they appear in all capitals", so any rendering that lowercases or reworders them drops the distinction — but that supports the mechanism, not the claim about what translators tend to do. The lesson's hedge "tends to" is appropriate; kind=opinion, non-blocking.

claim_verdicts.evidence: No docs root in versions.yaml prescribes where to search first. I read refs/kubernetes-website/content/en/docs/contribute/style/page-content-types.md and style-guide.md and searched refs/ for guidance on site-scoped versus web-wide search; nothing addresses it. The claim states a habit, not a measurement, and is registered kind=opinion, so this verdict does not block approval.

refs/rfc/rfc9111.txt:1081 "5.2. Cache-Control" — "The \"Cache-Control\" header field is used to list directives for caches along the request/response chain." The directive the script prints is defined at :1208 "5.2.2.1. max-age". So the defining page for this standard header is a specification section, i.e. a reference entry you search for. Note for the ledger: the claim carries version_key "http", which resolves to RFC 9110 in versions.yaml, but the governing document here is RFC 9111 — see issue on section 4.

The IETF case is evidenced: refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt front matter "Request for Comments: 9110", "STD: 97", "Obsoletes: 2818, 7230, 7231, ...", "Updates: 3864", and the abstract "This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, ..." — a number identifies the document and a new number supersedes the old one, instead of a selector switching page sets. But the claim is written of every specification, and neither refs/ nor any docs root in versions.yaml says specification pages generally carry no version selector.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A specification is published as one fixed, numbered document — a new number supersedes the old rather than the text being revised in place — so it has no version selector; its document number identifies it instead.

claim_verdicts.evidence: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-checkout, DESCRIPTION: "git checkout [--detach] <commit>: The same as `git checkout <branch>`, except that instead of pointing HEAD at the branch, it points HEAD at the commit ID", with SYNOPSIS "git checkout [<tree-ish>] [--detach] <commit>". A tag name is such a commit argument: in this repository the annotated tag object stage-0 inflates to "object ff911b0b… / type commit", and that commit is what the working tree holds. Section 2 omits detached HEAD — a simplification, not an error. Page is the current git-scm docs, behaviour unchanged at the pinned git 2.46.

issues.text: The stem names a specification, but keyed option (a) asks about the release the page was written for. Section 3 teaches that a specification "has no version selector" and section 7 repeats it, so by the lesson's own text an RFC has no release to be written for. A reader who applies the lesson can strike (a) and lose a select-all question whose key is [a, b, c]. The key is right for a product documentation page, not for the page this stem names.
issues.fix: Take the specification out of the stem: "The documentation page you found for that header says one thing, and `scripts/http/cache-headers.sh` at `stage-0` behaves as if it said another." Then option (d), en and vi, becomes "The page, which is what is wrong whenever it disagrees with a machine you can watch." Keep the key [a, b, c] and options (a), (b), (c), (e) unchanged.
issues.quote: The specification page for the header says one thing, and `scripts/http/cache-headers.sh` at `stage-0` behaves as if it said another.

issues.text: Same defect, second question. The stem is a header printed by cache-headers.sh; section 4 says the reference for a standard header is a specification and section 3 says a specification "has no version selector", yet step (a) of the ordering is "Move the version selector to the release you are running". The required order therefore contains a step the lesson says does not exist in this scenario, so a reader who followed the lesson cannot place it with confidence.
issues.fix: Reword option (a) to cover both cases, keeping the key [b, d, a, e, c]: en "Line up the release the page describes with the release you run — move the version selector, or note the document's number if the page has none."; vi "Khớp bản phát hành trang mô tả với bản bạn đang chạy — chuyển bộ chọn phiên bản, hoặc ghi lại số hiệu tài liệu nếu trang không có bộ chọn."
issues.quote: Move the version selector to the release you are running.

issues.text: The gloss ends with an unconditional "it has no version selector". The evidence reaches the IETF case only — RFC 9110 is one fixed numbered document that obsoletes its predecessors rather than being revised in place — and no docs root in versions.yaml states this of specifications in general; families that publish dated or numbered editions are not covered. Claim 20 is verdicted rephrased for the same reason.
issues.fix: Write: "specification — the standards document that defines something with no single product behind it, such as an HTTP header; it is a reference, and — being one fixed, numbered document — it has no version selector." Update claim 20 in .meta.json to the same condition.
issues.quote: it is a reference, and it has no version selector.

issues.text: Ledger bookkeeping: claim 19 carries version_key "http", which content/versions.yaml resolves to https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110, but Cache-Control and max-age are defined in RFC 9111 sections 5.2 and 5.2.2.1. As pinned, the claim's own version_key does not point at the document that decides it, so the next reviewer cannot check it from the declared root. The lesson body never names an RFC, so nothing in the prose is wrong.
issues.fix: Either add a standards key http_caching with docs https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111 to content/versions.yaml and point claim 19 at it, or change the standards.http docs entry to the HTTP document set (RFC 9110/9111/9112). Then update claim 19's version_key and source_hint to match.
